questions.question: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components in React?
questions.title: Controlled Vs Uncontrolled
questions.direct_answer: Controlled: form input value comes from React state — `<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)}/>` — React is the single source of truth. Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value, React reads it via ref on demand — `<input defaultValue="x" ref={inputRef}/>` — the DOM is the source of truth.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Controlled: form input value comes from React state — `<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)}/>` — React is the single source of truth. Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value, React reads it via ref on demand — `<input defaultValue="x" ref={inputRef}/>` — the DOM is the source of truth.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph controlled
        K[keystroke] --> OC[onChange] --> SS[setState] --> RR[re-render]
        RR --> IV[input.value = state]
    end
    subgraph uncontrolled
        K2[keystroke] --> DOM[DOM updates itself]
        DOM -.read on submit.-> REF[ref.current.value]
    end
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why controlled exists at all (the design reason): React's contract is UI = f(state). If the DOM can hold its own value, the UI shows something state doesn't describe — the model breaks. Controlled inputs close that hole: every displayed character exists in state, so validation, clearing, programmatic setting (form prefill from server data), and reset are all just state operations.

The uncontrolled performance win, quantified (the depth that impresses): a controlled input re-renders the component (and by default its children) on every keystroke. In a form with 30 inputs where each re-renders a heavy sibling tree, keystrokes get janky. Uncontrolled inputs skip this entirely — the browser's native fast path handles typing, and React never knows until submit. This is why react-hook-form (uncontrolled core) benchmarks orders of magnitude faster than controlled-everything for large forms.

The migration pattern (the practical follow-up): converting uncontrolled → controlled mid-flight causes the 'input won't type' bug — value={state} with no onChange makes the input read-only. The fix pair: always supply onChange with a controlled value. The defaultValue → value switch is one-way at runtime: once controlled, defaultValue is ignored.
